courses.title: Data Structures & Algorithms
courses.blurb: From what an algorithm is to advanced graphs, tries, greedy, intervals and advanced dynamic programming: every idea explained from first principles, with diagrams, code in several languages, complexity tables and practice problems.
courses.intro:
## How this course works

Each lesson follows the same shape, so you always know where you are:

1. **Intuition** in plain words, with a picture, before any code.
2. **How it works**, step by step on a small example.
3. **Code** you can read in JavaScript, Python, Java or C++ (pick a tab).
4. **Complexity** as a table: what each operation costs in time and space, and why.
5. **Practice**: hand-picked problems from the PrepOS problem bank, then a three-question check.

## How to study

- Go in order the first time. Later chapters assume the earlier ones.
- Read the intuition, then **close the page and try to explain it aloud** before reading the code.
- Type the code yourself. Reading code feels like understanding; typing it is understanding.
- Solve the linked problems before moving on. A lesson is only really done when you can solve a problem that uses it.
- Mark a lesson done only after the check. Your progress here is separate from your daily plan and never affects your streak.

## The big picture

Almost every interview problem is one of a few **patterns** on top of a few **data structures**. The chapters go: measuring cost (Big-O), then arrays and hashing, then the pointer and window patterns, binary search, and onward to trees, graphs and dynamic programming.

courses.title: System Design (HLD + LLD)
courses.blurb: Every system design topic taught twice, high-level and low-level: building blocks, data and messaging, reliability, distributed systems (consensus, transactions, CAP) and full interview case studies.
courses.audience: Backend engineers preparing for design interviews
courses.intro:
## HLD and LLD, side by side

Interviewers ask system design in two flavours, and good engineers need both:

- **HLD (high-level design)**: boxes and arrows. Which services, databases, caches and queues? How does it scale to millions of users? What breaks, and what do you trade away?
- **LLD (low-level design)**: classes and code. What are the entities, interfaces and design patterns? How do you make it thread-safe and testable?

Every lesson here has an **HLD** tab and an **LLD** tab for the same topic, so you learn how the big picture turns into real code.

## How to use it

1. Read the HLD tab and try to sketch the diagram yourself first.
2. Read the LLD tab and implement the core classes from memory.
3. Take the check, then open the matching case study under System Design for a full 45-minute mock.

Numbers to keep in mind throughout: a server handles roughly thousands of requests per second, memory is about 100 ns, SSD about 100 us, a cross-region network hop about 100 ms.

courses.title: Frontend Engineering at Scale
courses.blurb: How the browser really works, rendering strategies, React in depth (rendering model, Server Components, concurrency), Core Web Vitals and performance, testing, accessibility and security, and frontend architecture at scale.
courses.audience: Frontend and full-stack engineers going from mid-level to senior
courses.intro:
## What this course is for

Most frontend interviews past the junior level stop asking what a hook does and start asking **why**: why the page is slow, why this rendering strategy, why this state library, how fifty engineers ship one frontend without breaking each other. This course teaches the reasoning behind those answers.

## How each lesson works

1. **Concepts** in plain words, with a diagram, before any code.
2. **How it works** underneath: what the browser, the framework or the build tool actually does.
3. **In code**: TypeScript and React you can read and type yourself.
4. **Interview**: the questions senior candidates get, with model answers.
5. A three-question **check** before you mark the lesson done.

## How to study

- Chapter 1 (the browser and rendering) is the foundation; take it in order.
- Chapter 2 (architecture at scale) is what separates senior answers. Read it alongside the *Frontend at scale* and *Frontend system design* tracks under Web & AI, and build one of their projects.
- After each lesson, close the page and explain the main diagram out loud in two minutes. If you cannot, read it again.

Your progress here is separate from the daily plan and never affects your streak.

courses.title: GenAI End to End
courses.blurb: From how an LLM turns tokens into the next token, through training and serving, to RAG in depth, agents and tool calling with MCP, and shipping safely with evals, observability, guardrails and cost control.
courses.intro:
## What this course is for

AI-engineer interviews now mix three kinds of question: **how the model works** (attention, training, sampling, the KV cache), **how to build with it** (RAG, tools, agents) and **how to ship it** (evals, safety, cost and latency). This course covers all three in the order you need them.

## How each lesson works

1. **Concepts** first, with diagrams and small worked examples.
2. **Under the hood**: the maths and the systems, explained in plain words with shapes and numbers.
3. **In code**: Python and TypeScript you can run and change.
4. **Interview**: questions and model answers.
5. A three-question **check** before you mark it done.

## How to study

- Chapter 1 explains the model. You do not need to train one, but you must be able to explain the forward pass, why the KV cache exists and what temperature does.
- Chapter 2 is about building. Pair it with the *RAG and AI search* and *GenAI engineering* tracks under Web & AI, and build the RAG assistant or the research agent project: an AI project with real evals is the strongest resume line right now.
- The field moves fast. The ideas here are stable; check provider docs for the exact API details before you use them.

Your progress here is separate from the daily plan and never affects your streak.
